summary: Module 7 REFLECT. Writing the bad postmortem's critique and then rewriting it revealed how the skill decomposes: blamelessness is not etiquette, it is an information-incentive structure (people hide mistakes when blamed, so reports starve of data); root cause must be systemic or it cannot be fixed (if John had tested locally and the index still dropped at production scale, the same incident recurs -- the real root cause is the missing staging gate); contributing factors must be system gaps, not person-actions; remediations must be owned, deadlined, and checkable ('CI blocks merge' vs 'developers should test'); and the timeline must be precise enough to find where time was lost. The most important transferable discipline: critique someone else's work to find your own blind spots -- my first postmortem had owners but no deadlines and qualitative impact, both fixed after I read the bad one with fresh eyes. The S3 standard now feels automatic: every remediation I write must pass 'does this change the system, or just ask a person to be better?'. Postmortem writing is a debugging technique for the organization, not paperwork.
evidence: Full anti-pattern critique of the fictional postmortem (blame, vague timeline, symptom root cause, person factors, unmeasured impact, non-executable remediations)
Complete blameless rewrite with systemic root cause, system-gap CFs, precise UTC timeline, owned/deadlined/checkable R1-R5
Own postmortem upgraded: deadlines + measured Impact section added after self-critique
